Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
The event happened because of the way I acted
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette:
Marisol is a 27-year-old Latina animator who came to treatment months after ending a relationship in which her boyfriend physically abused her. When she speaks about the relationship, she does not describe one isolated incident so much as a series of moments that narrowed her life and changed how she now sees herself. The episode she returns to most often happened late at night in the apartment they had shared, after an argument that began over something minor and quickly became frightening. She remembers the speed with which his face changed, the sound of his voice getting louder, and then being grabbed and hit while she tried first to argue back and then to make herself small. What stays with her is not only the pain and fear but the sense that, in those minutes, she stopped recognizing herself. She recalls pleading with him, trying to calm him, saying things she now cannot bear to repeat because they feel humiliating and unlike the person she believed herself to be. Looking back, she is preoccupied by the idea that the assault happened because of the way she acted. She goes over the argument repeatedly, convinced that if she had spoken differently, not challenged him, not stayed, or left sooner, it would not have happened.

In the weeks after the relationship ended, Marisol found that the event did not settle into the past. She would be pulled back into it without warning, not as a story she could calmly tell, but as something that seemed to happen again in pieces. A man's raised voice in the hallway outside her apartment or the sharp sound of a door hitting a frame could make her body go rigid before she had even fully registered what she had heard. Sometimes, when a scene she was animating required characters to argue or make sudden aggressive movements, she would freeze at her desk and feel overwhelmed by fragments of that night. She understood these reactions as proof that something in her had been permanently altered. She had come to believe that the abuse had changed her for the worse, that she was now someone more fragile, more fearful, and less able to trust her own judgment. It frightened her how quickly she could go from concentrating on a project to feeling as if she were no longer in the studio at all.

Her work as an animator, once a source of absorption and pride, became one of the places where her distress was most visible. She works in a collaborative environment where storyboards are reviewed aloud and scenes are refined in groups. She began dreading meetings, especially when feedback grew animated or someone interrupted sharply, because even ordinary creative tension felt dangerous to her body. She started keeping her camera off during remote calls when she could, speaking less in reviews, and volunteering less for action-heavy sequences. To coworkers, she likely appeared distracted or withdrawn, but internally she was trying to prevent herself from being overtaken. After difficult workdays she would go home exhausted and ashamed, telling herself that she had become weak.

Marisol's guilt has settled around more than the assault itself. What troubles her almost as much is how she behaved in order to survive the relationship. She says she tolerated things she never imagined she would tolerate, lied to friends about what was happening, and shaped herself around his moods. She had always thought of herself as direct, independent, and unwilling to let anyone control her. Now she is haunted by the belief that she acted in ways that go against who she is. She does not describe those choices with compassion or context; instead she speaks about them as evidence of a moral failure. She is harsh with herself for staying, harsh with herself for pleading, and harsh with herself for the silence that followed. In her mind, these moments mean something troubling about her character.

Over time her world has become smaller. She is single now, but this has not felt like freedom so much as distance. She keeps conversations light, avoids any situation that might lead to dating, and is watchful with men in ways she never used to be. Even with friends, she often holds back, anticipating judgment if she tells the full story. The more she has tried to manage on her own, the more convinced she has become that this version of her is permanent. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent incident at work when a colleague, frustrated with a technical delay, slapped a hand against a table and raised his voice. Marisol abruptly left the room, locked herself in a restroom, and cried in a way that felt to her both uncontrollable and deeply embarrassing. Afterward she was shaken not only by the intensity of the reaction but by the thought, "This is who I am now."

By the time she comes in, Marisol is torn between fear and hope. What frightens her most is the possibility that the abuse has irreversibly damaged her and that, beneath everything else, she was somehow responsible for what happened. What she hopes for, more quietly, is not to erase the past but to be able to remember it without feeling swallowed by it, and to find some way to look at herself that is not organized entirely around blame.
